notes.title: Start here: a support desk's SLA clocks and escalation sweep
notes.body:
This pack uses a support-desk app (Next.js, Prisma, PostgreSQL). Tickets have deadlines (an SLA: a first-response deadline and a resolution deadline). A background *sweep* escalates tickets that are overdue, and staff can assign and move tickets between support groups. The course follows a ticket through route, validation, service, repository and audit log.

Reading order, from the course README (about five hours in two sittings):

1. `astraupskill/01-CODEBASE-MAP.md`: where routes, services, repositories and tests live.
2. `astraupskill/02-CONCEPTS.md`: SLA clocks, escalation rules and the `undefined` versus `null` trap.
3. `astraupskill/03-WORKED-CHANGE.md` and `04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING.md`.
4. `astraupskill/05-PRACTICE.md`: six prediction exercises. Write your answers before reading chapter 6.
5. `astraupskill/06-SOLUTIONS-AND-REVIEW.md`: most quizzes come from here.

Code to keep open: `src/services/escalationService.ts`, `src/services/ticketService.ts` and `src/repositories/ticketRepository.ts`.

notes.title: undefined versus null in a Prisma update
notes.body:
In a Prisma `update`, each key in `data` is an instruction for one column. JavaScript has two "empty" values, `undefined` and `null`, and Prisma treats them differently. Look up in the Prisma documentation exactly what each one does as a value in `data`, before you read the repository.

Then follow one optional field, `assigneeId`, all the way from the request schema through the service to the repository, and note at every hop which of the two values it can be when the client omits the field and when the client sends `null`. The repository code in this project handles each column with an explicit expression; read it with your Prisma notes beside it. Also note what the service itself adds to the update when a ticket moves between groups.

The SLA side of the pack also needs careful reading of small helpers. Look at `overdueMinutes` in `escalationService.ts` (lines 16-18) and work out by hand what it returns for a few deadlines in the past and the future. Then read how `runSweep` picks which deadline (`dueAt`) is the active one.

excerpts.quote: assigneeId: (input.assigneeId === undefined ? undefined : input.assigneeId) as any,

notes.title: Why a 'constructor' role breaks the one-line permission check
notes.body:
**Key: the lookup finds the inherited Object constructor, so .includes throws and a 403 becomes a 500.**

`roleCapabilities` is a plain object literal, so it inherits properties from `Object.prototype`, such as `constructor` and `toString`. `roleCapabilities["constructor"]` is therefore the `Object` function, not `undefined`. Optional chaining (`?.`) only stops on `null`/`undefined`, so it carries on and calls `.includes` on a function, which does not have that method: a `TypeError`. The route turns the crash into a 500 instead of a clean 403. The shipped code checks `hasOwnProperty` and `Array.isArray` first and returns `false`.

Why the others are wrong:
- *TypeScript rejects it at runtime*: TypeScript types do not exist at runtime.
- *Optional chaining treats inherited properties as undefined*: it does not; the inherited value is a real function.
- *It returns true*: it throws before returning anything.

excerpts.quote: A session carrying `role: "constructor"` makes `roleCapabilities["constructor"]` resolve to the `Object` constructor function — not `undefined` — so the optional chain does not short-circuit and `.includes` throws a `TypeError`, which the route turns into a 500 instead of a 403.
if (!Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(roleCapabilities, user.role)) { return false; }

notes.title: WHERE escalatedAt IS NULL lets only one sweep win
notes.body:
**Key: the conditional update's WHERE escalatedAt IS NULL, which one write can match.**

`markEscalated` runs `updateMany` with `where: { id, escalatedAt: null, ... }` and sets `escalatedAt`. The database applies the two updates one after the other. The first finds `escalatedAt` still NULL, matches the row and sets it. The second now finds `escalatedAt` set, matches 0 rows, and gets `null` back. That is compare-and-set.

Why the others are wrong:
- *A unique index on escalatedAt*: there is no such index, and a unique timestamp would not express "escalate once" anyway.
- *Prisma serializes calls*: Prisma sends separate queries; it does not queue updates per id.
- *An in-process mutex*: two workers may be separate processes, and the code has no lock; the guarantee comes from the `where`.

excerpts.quote: const result = await prisma.ticket.updateMany({ where: { id: input.ticketId, escalatedAt: null, ...(input.expectedStatus ? { status: input.expectedStatus } : {}) },
// one escalation per ticket, and only from the status the sweep saw

notes.title: The id tie-break makes rule choice repeatable
notes.body:
**Key: so rules with equal thresholds route a ticket the same way on each sweep run.**

The sort is `b.afterMins - a.afterMins || a.id.localeCompare(b.id)`: biggest threshold first, and if two rules have the same threshold, the difference is 0, so `||` falls through to comparing ids. Without that second part, two rules with equal `afterMins` would stay in whatever order the database returned them, which is not guaranteed. The same ticket could then go to different groups on two runs over the same data, and a failing test could not be reproduced.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Ids encode creation time, older rules win*: the guide gives no such policy; the point is a fixed order.
- *localeCompare is faster*: it only runs on a tie; speed is not the reason.
- *Smallest threshold first*: the sort is descending, so the greatest eligible threshold is chosen.

excerpts.quote: .sort((a, b) => b.afterMins - a.afterMins || a.id.localeCompare(b.id))[0];
so the same ticket could route to different groups on two runs over identical data. A deterministic tie-break makes the sweep reproducible — and makes a failing test reproducible too.

notes.title: Leaving out assigneeId keeps the current assignee
notes.body:
**Key: untouched, because undefined leaves the column alone in the update.**

The request never mentions `assigneeId`, so it is `undefined`, which in this code means "no change". In the service, `input.assigneeId === undefined ? ticket.assigneeId : input.assigneeId` keeps the current assignee as the next value. In the repository, each column is written only when its input is not `undefined`; Prisma leaves a column with an `undefined` value alone. Either way the assignee column ends up as it was. To clear it, the client must send `{ assigneeId: null, reason: "clear" }`.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Rejected, assigneeId is required*: it is optional; omitting it is a valid "keep".
- *Set to the requester*: `reason` is a note, not an instruction to pick a user.
- *Coerced to null*: nothing turns `undefined` into `null`; that would clear the assignee.

excerpts.quote: let nextAssigneeId = input.assigneeId === undefined ? ticket.assigneeId : input.assigneeId;
`{ reason: "keep" }` therefore reaches `assign` with `assigneeId: undefined` and the column is untouched.

notes.title: overdueMinutes floors to whole minutes and never goes negative
notes.body:
**Key: 1 and 0: it floors complete minutes and clamps future deadlines to zero.**

The function is `Math.max(0, Math.floor((now - dueAt) / 60_000))`.

- 89 seconds ago: 89,000 ms / 60,000 = 1.48, and `Math.floor` gives 1.
- 10 minutes in the future: now minus dueAt is -600,000 ms, so -10, and `Math.max(0, -10)` gives 0.

Why the others are wrong:
- *1 and -10*: `Math.max(0, ...)` removes negative values.
- *2 and -10*: `Math.floor` rounds down, not to the nearest, and negatives are clamped.
- *1.48 and 0*: `Math.floor` removes the fraction.

excerpts.quote: return Math.max(0, Math.floor((now.getTime() - dueAt.getTime()) / 60_000));
`overdueMinutes` floors complete minutes and clamps future values to zero.

notes.title: A boolean in a fake does not prove database concurrency
notes.body:
**Key: only the service's control flow against a fake, not a database race.**

The fake stores `claimed = true` after the first call and refuses the second. That proves the service handles a "you lost" answer correctly: no second escalation, no second audit. It cannot prove that the real `updateMany ... WHERE escalatedAt IS NULL` behaves that way in PostgreSQL under two simultaneous workers, because no database is involved. The solutions chapter asks you to state that limit whenever you quote the test.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Ticket and audit in one transaction*: the fake has no transaction; the guide says the rollback test also does not prove PostgreSQL rolled back.
- *Nothing; delete the test*: the guide calls it "useful for service control flow".
- *Race-safe against real PostgreSQL*: that needs a real database test.

excerpts.quote: A test that sets `claimed = true` and then calls the same fake twice proves only that the fake remembers a boolean. It is useful for service control flow, but it is not database concurrency evidence.

notes.title: Invalid target versus lost race: two different no-escalation paths
notes.body:
**Key: the invalid target stops before markEscalated, and the race loser gets null.**

In `runSweep`, an invalid target (no such group, or a customer as target user) hits a `continue` before any write: the ticket is skipped and `markEscalated` is never called. A race loser passes all checks, calls `markEscalated`, and the conditional update matches 0 rows, so it gets `null`. Neither writes an audit row, but for different reasons, and the guide says to test both because refactors tend to break one of them.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Indistinguishable, same error*: neither path raises an error; one never writes, the other gets `null`.
- *Both call markEscalated*: the invalid target is skipped before the call.
- *Invalid target audited; loser throws 500*: the guide warns against exactly those two refactors.

excerpts.quote: an invalid target is skipped before `markEscalated`, while a concurrent loser reaches it and receives null. Both produce no audit for different reasons.
const targetGroup = await this.deps.supportGroupRepository.findById(targetGroupId); if (!targetGroup) { continue; }

notes.title: Moving a ticket's group clears an incompatible assignee
notes.body:
**Key: the group move together with an explicit null assigneeId.**

When `supportGroupId` is sent and the ticket has an assignee, `assignTicket` loads that assignee. Their group (g1) differs from the new group (g2), so `nextAssigneeId` becomes `null`. The repository then receives both the new group and `assigneeId: null`, and clears the assignee. Without this, the ticket would sit in g2 with a g1 user attached, and no group-scoped list would show it to anyone: an invisible ticket.

Why the others are wrong:
- *The assignee is transferred to g2*: the code does not change users' groups.
- *A 409 demanding a new assignee*: the code clears the assignee instead of refusing.
- *Only the group move*: that is the old "before" behaviour the concepts guide describes.

excerpts.quote: if (input.supportGroupId && nextAssigneeId) { const currentAssignee = await this.deps.userRepository.findById(nextAssigneeId); if (currentAssignee?.supportGroupId && currentAssignee.supportGroupId !== nextGroupId) { nextAssigneeId = null; } }
Moving to `g2` while the assignee belongs to `g1` would leave routing state that no group-scoped list query returns

notes.title: A lost assignment race: a retry message and no audit
notes.body:
**Key: a ValidationDomainError asking to retry, without an assignment audit.**

`assign` returns `null` when `updateMany` changed 0 rows (`result.count` is 0). The service checks that straight away: `if (!updated) throw new ValidationDomainError("Ticket changed before assignment; retry the request")`. The audit write comes on the next lines, so it never runs. The loser finds out from the row count, and the audit log only records assignments that actually happened.

Why the others are wrong:
- *A silent 200 with the stale ticket*: the service throws instead of returning.
- *Success plus a conflict audit*: no audit is written on this path.
- *A database exception and a 500*: a zero-row update is not a database error; the code turns it into a domain error on purpose.

excerpts.quote: if (!updated) throw new ValidationDomainError("Ticket changed before assignment; retry the request"); await this.deps.auditLogRepository.create({
return result.count ? this.findById(input.ticketId) as Promise<RepoTicket> : null;

notes.title: Exactly at the threshold, the rule fires
notes.body:
**Key: it escalates: 30 breached minutes meets afterMins <= breachedMinutes.**

The ticket is unanswered, so the active deadline is the earliest one, 11:30. At 12:00, `overdueMinutes` gives exactly 30 (1,800,000 ms / 60,000, no fraction to floor). The rule filter is `candidate.afterMins <= breachedMinutes`, and 30 <= 30 is true, so the rule is eligible and the ticket escalates once.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Needs strictly more than 30*: the comparison is `<=`, so the boundary is included.
- *Rounds down to 29*: 30 whole minutes is exactly 30; flooring changes nothing.
- *Escalates twice*: the sweep picks one deadline and one rule, and `escalatedAt` allows one escalation per ticket.

excerpts.quote: .filter((candidate) => candidate.afterMins <= breachedMinutes)
With current time 12:00, first response due 11:30 and a 30-minute rule, `overdueMinutes` returns exactly 30 and `afterMins <= breachedMinutes` is true, so the sweep escalates.

notes.title: Once answered, only the resolution clock counts
notes.body:
**Key: no: once answered, only the future resolution clock counts toward a breach.**

`runSweep` picks `dueAt` like this: if `firstResponseAt` is set, use `resolutionDueAt`; otherwise use the earliest of the two deadlines. This ticket was answered at 11:45, so `dueAt` is the resolution deadline, 13:00. At 12:00 that is in the future, so `dueAt > now` and the loop `continue`s: no escalation. The first-response deadline that was missed earlier no longer matters.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Yes, first response was breached by 30 minutes*: an answered ticket ignores that clock.
- *The earliest deadline is always active*: only while the ticket is unanswered.
- *No, needs strictly more than 30*: the comparison is inclusive; the real reason is the future resolution deadline.

excerpts.quote: const dueAt = ticket.firstResponseAt ? ticket.resolutionDueAt : [ticket.firstResponseDueAt, ticket.resolutionDueAt]
An answered ticket ignores its first response deadline, so a future resolution deadline produces no escalation.

notes.title: The first reply to commit sets firstResponseAt
notes.body:
**Key: the first to commit, as the second update matches zero rows.**

`markFirstResponse` updates with `where: { id, firstResponseAt: null }`. The first reply's update finds the column empty and fills it. The second reply's update now finds the column set, so the condition fails, 0 rows change, and the method returns `null`. The stored time is the first writer's. The concepts guide describes the change: before, it "always writes the new timestamp"; after, "the first writer wins".

Why the others are wrong:
- *The later one, last write wins*: that was the old behaviour without the `firstResponseAt: null` condition.
- *Earlier client timestamp compared in SQL*: the `where` compares the column to `null`, not two timestamps.
- *Both*: there is one column, and the second write is refused.

excerpts.quote: where: { id: input.ticketId, firstResponseAt: null }, data: { firstResponseAt: input.firstResponseAt }
Before: a first response update always writes the new timestamp. After: the repository requires `firstResponseAt: null`, so the first writer wins.
